newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai finance minister says worst over.
newsitem.headline: Thai finance minister says worst over.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan on Monday said the worst was over in Thailand's financial crisis and he was confident of renewed economic growth.

"I feel confident that we have weathered the worst of the domestic economic instability and the downturn in the global and regional business cycle," Amnuay said in a speech to international business executives.
"The Thai road to economic restructuring and adjustment looks set to be smoother in the future," he said.
Thai authorities, concerned by the poor health of financial institutions, ordered them to raise capital and to set aside more provisions for sub-standard assets.
The moves rocked the financial industry, sparking a run on deposits and causing the stock market to plummet to near five-year lows as investors worried about the economy dumped shares.
A package of measures, including plans to rescue troubled property developers and their financiers through a multi-billion dollar bond issue, helped restore some confidence.

"We have implemented some tough policies and made some painful decisions," Amnuay said. "But we have persevered and worked hard to put in place the measures and institutions necessary to facilitate the economic and business transition to the next millennium."
"To regain confidence at the macroeconomic level, the present administration is committed to cautious demand management policies, supported by prudent fiscal and monetary measures," he said.
Amnuay said economic indicators looked positive and he was convinced 1997 would be a better year than 1996.
"In sum, I foresee the beginning of a new era of growth with stability for the Thai economy," Amnuay said.
Thailand projects its current account deficit will narrow sharply to 6.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year from 8.2 percent in 1996.
The economy, in terms of GDP, is pegged to grow by 6.8 percent and exports are projected to rise by seven to 10 percent, Amnuay said.
He said the economy was undergoing a structural shift from a manufacturer of labour- or resource-intensive products to higher-value-added goods.

"And while the stagnant export growth last year resulted largely from cyclical factors, it also underlined the need to strengthen our competitiveness in the face of higher domestic labour costs, emerging competitors in regional markets, and increasing global competition," he said.
In 1996 exports dropped 0.2 percent while imports grew about 2.3 percent.

Amnuay said foreign investment would be a key element of its technology upgrading programmes. More than half of the approved investments in 1996 of more than $20 billion were in export-oriented projects, he said.
Amnuay also repeated the government's vow to defend the Thai baht and maintain the currency's stability by keeping the current exchange rate system.
"The present exchange rate system has been the anchor of growth and stability for the past 13 years and has helped to encourage steady foreign direct investment inflows," he said.
